record.paper_title: Some open problems in mathematical relativity
record.original_question: To what extent is the analogy between apparent horizons and minimal surfaces valid, including whether a meaningful second-variation or stability theory for apparent horizons exists even though no functional is known whose Euler-Lagrange equations are the apparent-horizon equations?

evidence.quote: To what extent is this analogy valid? Unlike the area functional and minimal surfaces, there is no known functional for which the apparent horizon equations arise as the Euler-Lagrange equations. Does the "second variation" formula for apparent horizons mean anything?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g,K)$ be a smooth spacelike Cauchy initial data set in a four-dimensional spacetime, where $g$ is a Riemannian metric on the 3-manifold $M$ and $K$ is the second fundamental form. For a smooth, closed, two-sided hypersurface $\Sigma \subset M$ with outward unit normal $\nu$, let $H$ denote the mean curvature of $\Sigma$ in $(M,g)$ and let $\mathrm{tr}_\Sigma K$ denote the trace of $K$ along $\Sigma$. The outgoing null expansion is $\theta^+ := H + \mathrm{tr}_\Sigma K$, and $\Sigma$ is called an apparent horizon (a marginally outer trapped surface) if $\theta^+ \equiv 0$.

Unlike minimal surfaces (where $H=0$ are critical points of the area functional), no functional is known whose Euler–Lagrange equations are the apparent-horizon equations $\theta^+ = 0$. Nevertheless, by analogy with the minimal surface theory one can attempt to define and use a notion of "stability" and a "second variation" for apparent horizons.

Determine the extent to which the analogy between apparent horizons and minimal surfaces is mathematically valid. In particular:

(a) Decide whether there exists a meaningful variational principle whose Euler–Lagrange equations coincide with $\theta^+ = 0$.

(b) Develop a stability/second-variation theory for apparent horizons that plays the role of the second variation of area for minimal surfaces, identifying to what extent its spectral and geometric consequences (existence of stable apparent horizons, area estimates, foliations by apparent horizons, rigidity, etc.) parallel those of minimal surface theory.
artifact.status_search_result: A substantial stability theory for marginally outer trapped surfaces (apparent horizons) was developed by Andersson, Mars, and Simon (PRL 2005; Adv. Theor. Math. Phys. 2008), who introduced a (non-self-adjoint) stability operator $L_v$ whose principal eigenvalue plays a role analogous to the second variation of area for minimal surfaces, and used it to prove existence of marginally outer trapped tubes and area/rigidity results. Subsequent work (e.g., Galloway–Schoen on topology of horizons, Eichmair on Plateau-type existence, free-boundary MOTS) has extended the analogy considerably. However, no variational/functional formulation whose Euler–Lagrange equation is $\theta^+ = 0$ is known, so the question is only partially resolved.

status_evidence.title: Stability of marginally outer trapped surfaces and existence of marginally outer trapped tubes
status_evidence.snippet: We introduce the stability operator $L_v$ for MOTS and characterize stable MOTS via sign conditions on its principal eigenvalue; strictly stable MOTS extend to marginally outer trapped tubes.
status_evidence.claim: A second-variation-like stability theory for apparent horizons exists and yields results paralleling minimal surface theory.

status_evidence.title: Stable surfaces and free boundary marginally outer trapped surfaces
status_evidence.snippet: Develops free boundary theory for MOTS following the minimal surface analogy.
status_evidence.claim: The minimal-surface analogy continues to be extended, including free boundary versions.

status_evidence.title: The Area of Horizons and the Trapped Region
status_evidence.snippet: Uses the stability notion for MOTS to derive area and trapped-region results.
status_evidence.claim: Stability for MOTS yields meaningful geometric/area consequences in analogy with minimal surfaces.
